extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and classical literature; educators and writers interested in Plato's theory of education and the arts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for literature, music, education, and art appropriate to Plato's ideal city (as discussed in the Republic). Useful for authors or educators seeking to craft moral, civic, and pedagogically-suitable works in that paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of nursery tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Children hear stories before they learn gymnastics, and the stories are either untrue or have at most 'one or two grains of truth' in a bushel of falsehood; early life is very impressible and children ought not to learn what they will have to unlearn when they grow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must lay down principles according to which books are to be written; banish improper tales (examples: Homer and Hesiod's accounts such as Uranus and Saturn, Zeus beating his father, Hephaestus binding his mother). If allowed at all, such stories should be confined to mysteries and not told plainly to the young. The goal is to prevent inculcation of immoral patterns (e.g., children encouraged to beat their fathers or quarrel) and to ensure that early tales have a good moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the gods as authors of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God must be represented as he is; not as the author of all things good and evil, but as author of good only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid poets to claim gods cause wrongdoing or sin (examples to suppress: Athene and Zeus inciting Pandarus; God causing Niobe's sufferings or the Trojan war). Such portrayals are 'wicked, suicidal fiction' and should not be uttered to old or young. The representation of divinity must support moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: God is unchangeable and true
rubrics_metrics.description: With God is no variableness or change of form; God remains forever fairest and best in his own image and does not change for good or ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetic inventions that show gods in disguises or changing forms (e.g., gods 'prowl about at night in strange disguises'); gods should not be depicted as deceitful or subject to passions and follies. This principle underpins censorship of offending myths and dramatizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: lie in the soul (worst) vs lie in words (permitted medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'lie in the soul' is the corruption of the highest truth (involuntary ignorance or asserting the greatest untruth) and is morally catastrophic; by contrast the 'lie in words' is a lower kind of deception usable as an accommodation or medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proscriptions: avoid doctrines that constitute a lie in the soul (examples: representing God as immoral, Protagoras's 'knowledge is sensation', Thrasymachus's 'might is right'). Allow limited, carefully controlled falsehoods (economies) employed by rulers only, when they have a clearly good moral effect and are necessary for educating the young or preserving the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge fear-inducing and lamenting portrayals (esp. of the afterlife)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to banish fear and cultivate courage, expunge passages that depict the underworld as horrifying or that incite fear of death or excessive lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove or alter graphic Tartarean nomenclature, images of squalid mansions and despairing shades, and verses that encourage lamentation (e.g., Achilles' preference for servitude over ruling the dead). Such material is unsuitable for soldiers/guardians and corrupts temperance and courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach temperance and self-control; forbid praise of gluttony, bribery, sexual license
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth must be temperate: temperance consists in self-control and obedience to authority; poetic or narrative praise of eating, drinking, sexual exploits, taking bribes, or meanness is to be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban verses that praise conviviality or drunkenness, erotic excess, or meanness (examples: Homeric praises of eating/drinking, Zeus' amorous exploits, Achilles taking gifts, Phoenix's advice to seek money). The aim is to cultivate citizens who resist bribery and base pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on imitating inferior or base characters; prefer descriptive style
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should not be imitators of meanness or baseness; the actor's mask tends to become his face. One man cannot rightly play many parts (e.g., both tragedy and comedy) without corrupting character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid dramatic imitation of women weeping, slaves, bullies, cowards, drunkards, animals, or obscene parts. Prefer the descriptive (narrative) style over dramatic imitation for guardians to avoid their adopting inferior traits. Restrict complex dramatic performances that encourage role-playing of base behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of allowed poetic subjects and styles for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetry is narrative (simple, imitative, or mixed), but for guardians the descriptive style with minimal imitation is preferred; if imitation occurs it must only be of the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tragedy/comedy where guardians would be required to imitate inferior roles; when imitation is allowed it must exemplify virtuous action. The state prefers 'rough, honest' poetry aligned with moral aims rather than theatrical complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical modes and instruments must be simple and morally suitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Music shapes the soul and must be purged of harmful modes and instruments; simplicity and suitability to the occasion are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban mixed Lydian harmonies and convivial Ionian or pure Lydian strains (associated with lamentation or indulgence). Allow Dorian (for war) and Phrygian (for peace, obedience, religious feeling). Prohibit complex many-stringed instruments and particularly the flute; permit lyre and harp in town and Pan's-pipe in the fields. Music must reflect harmony of soul and cultivate courage or obedience as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and rhythm must suit the subject and be simple
rubrics_metrics.description: A song has subject, harmony, and rhythm; metre and rhythm are dependent on subject and should be simple and appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple rhythmic ratios (noted: 3/2, 2/2, 2/1) and established martial, dactylic, trochaic, iambic measures as arranged to equalize syllables. Consult musical authority (Damon) for assignments of rhythms; avoid ornate or complex metres that disrupt the soul's simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and harmony as the overarching aesthetic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Across poetry, music, sculpture, and painting, simplicity and harmony should dominate so that citizens imbibe sweet and harmonious influences from all objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject unseemliness or deformity in art; the arts must help form a 'fair mind in the fair body.' Education by music is paramount as it reaches the innermost soul; visual arts must likewise conform to simplicity to avoid corrupting taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational method: imaginative formation first, reason later
rubrics_metrics.description: Children must be taught through imagination (including controlled fictions) in early life, developing gradually toward reasoning and truth as they mature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept limited use of fictions in youth when necessary for mental development, but restrict such uses to those with demonstrably good moral effects. Training proceeds from elements (letters/virtues) to their combinations; falsehoods used as pedagogical devices must be overseen by rulers and removed as understanding grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians' regimen: simple gymnastic, diet, and abstention from strong drink
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is related to the body; guardians require a simpler sort of gymnastic (awake, inured to hardships) and simple diet (Homeric model: roast meat, no fish or elaborate sauces); they must abstain from strong drink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid palaestra habits that encourage sleepiness or luxury. Forbid Sicilian cookery, Attic confections, and luxurious lifestyles that breed doctors and lawyers and dependence on medicinals or legalistic hair-splitting. A well-ordered State minimizes leisure for illness and discourages indulgent healthcare for moral reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glorifying luxury and the professions that feed on it
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury (sofas, tables, sauces, sweets) begets arts and services and eventually war and political evils; depictions or praise of luxury, gluttony, or professions born of excess (lawyers, physicians) should be suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create literature or cultural narratives that romanticize luxury or those who profit from it. Emphasize modest living and the civic harms of luxury (imports/exports leading to war, need for doctors and pleaders). This is part of moral-political education of citizens.
